notes.b: Living things are organised in levels of increasing complexity. Each level is made of units of the level below working together, so a whole organism can be understood by building up from its cells.
points: The order is cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. Learn it as a ladder: each step up combines the units of the step below.

Below the cell, cells are built of organelles (small structures inside the cell, each with a job), which are built of biomolecules (e.g. proteins, lipids). There is more on this in Structures and organelles of animal and plant cells.
Cell: the basic unit of life. In a multicellular organism (one made of many cells) cells are specialised (differentiated), so that the structure of each cell suits one job.
Tissue: a group of similar cells with the same structure, working together to carry out a particular function. Because the cells are alike, the tissue does one job well.
Organ: a structure made of several different tissues working together to carry out one or more functions. Having different tissues is what separates an organ from a tissue.
Organ system: a group of organs working together to carry out a major function, such as digesting food.
Organism: an individual living thing, whose organ systems work together to keep it alive.

Diagram: a five-step flow chart from cell to organism, with a human example at each level (muscle cell → muscle tissue → stomach → digestive system → human) and a plant example (xylem vessel → vascular tissue → leaf → shoot system → plant).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to put the levels in order and to define tissue, organ and organ system, with a human and a plant example of each. Remember that an organ contains several tissue types: blood is a tissue, not an organ, and the heart is an organ, not a tissue.

notes.b: A specialised cell has a structure that suits its particular job. Cells in a multicellular organism are specialised, and each example below links a feature of the cell to its function.
points: Unicellular organisms (those made of a single cell), e.g. Amoeba, yeast and bacteria, carry out every life process in one cell, so that cell is not specialised for a single job.
Differentiation: in a multicellular organism, all body cells contain the same DNA, but each cell type uses (expresses) only some of its genes, so cells become specialised.
Unspecialised cells that can still become several cell types are called stem cells. There is more on their uses in Genetic Engineering.

Red blood cell: no nucleus and a biconcave disc shape (a disc dipped in on both faces), giving more room for haemoglobin (the pigment that carries oxygen) and a large surface area for carrying oxygen.
Nerve cell (neuron): long thin extensions carry impulses (electrical signals) over long distances quickly, which suits a cell that links distant parts of the body.
Sperm cell: a tail for swimming, and many mitochondria in the middle section to release the energy that powers the tail.
Root hair cell: a long extension gives a large surface area for absorbing water and minerals from the soil.

Palisade cell of a leaf: packed with chloroplasts (the green structures where photosynthesis happens) for photosynthesis. Guard cells change shape to open and close the stomata (the pores in the leaf surface).
notes.tip: Exams ask how a named specialised cell suits its function. Name the feature and link it to the job, for example no nucleus and biconcave shape in a red blood cell give more haemoglobin and a large surface area for oxygen.

notes.b: Animal bodies are built from four main tissue types. Each is a group of similar cells doing one kind of job.
points: Epithelial tissue lines and covers surfaces, e.g. the lining of the gut and the skin surface.
Connective tissue supports and connects other tissues, e.g. bone, cartilage and blood. Blood counts as a connective tissue.
Muscle tissue contracts (shortens) to cause movement. There are three types: skeletal, smooth and cardiac (heart muscle).
Nervous tissue carries impulses, e.g. in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.
notes.tip: Blood is a tissue, not an organ. If asked to name animal tissue types, give all four: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.

notes.b: Plants also have tissue types, each a group of similar cells with one job. Together they build plant organs such as the leaf.
points: Dermal tissue is the epidermis, a protective outer layer covering the plant.
Vascular tissue carries materials around the plant: xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food.
Ground tissue makes up the bulk of the plant, carrying out photosynthesis and storage, e.g. the mesophyll (the inner tissue) of a leaf.
Meristematic tissue consists of dividing cells at root and shoot tips, where growth happens, so new cells for growth are made there.
A leaf contains dermal, ground and vascular tissue, which shows that an organ is made of several tissue types. Plant organs are root, stem, leaf and flower.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the plant tissue types (dermal, vascular, ground) and say where each is found, for example vascular tissue is xylem and phloem and ground tissue includes leaf mesophyll.

notes.b: Organs are made of several tissue types, and organs that cooperate form organ systems. Each system has one major function.
points: The stomach is an organ containing epithelial tissue lining it, smooth muscle that churns food, connective tissue and nervous tissue. Four different tissues working together make it an organ.
Other human organs include the heart, lungs, kidneys and brain.
Digestive system: breaks down and absorbs food. Circulatory system: transports materials around the body.
Breathing system: gas exchange (taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide). Nervous system: fast coordination.
Endocrine system: hormonal coordination. Musculoskeletal system: support and movement.
Urinary system: excretion (removing wastes) and water balance. Reproductive system: reproduction. Immune system: defence.
Plants have two systems. The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals.
The shoot system (stem, leaves and flowers) carries out photosynthesis, transport and reproduction.
notes.tip: Learn one function for each system and stay at that level of detail. Exams ask you to define an organ system and give a human and a plant example.

notes.h: Surface area to volume and the need for systems
notes.b: Size changes how a living thing gets what it needs. The bigger an organism, the harder it is to supply every cell, which is why large organisms need specialised systems.
points: As an organism gets bigger, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so its surface area to volume ratio falls.
Worked example: a 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm² and a volume of 1 cm³, a ratio of 6:1. A 2 cm cube has a surface area of 24 cm² and a volume of 8 cm³, a ratio of 3:1.
A unicellular organism has a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion across its membrane is enough to supply oxygen and food and to remove wastes.
In a large multicellular organism most cells are far from the surface, so diffusion alone is too slow to reach them.

Multicellular organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces (lungs, gut lining, root hairs, leaves) to take in materials, and transport systems (blood and heart; xylem and phloem) to carry them to every cell.
They also need coordination systems (nervous and hormonal) that link all the parts and keep conditions constant (homeostasis).
Division of labour: each cell type does one job very efficiently, but no cell can survive alone, so the cells depend on each other.
notes.tip: If asked why large organisms need transport systems, link it to surface area to volume: the ratio falls as size increases, so diffusion alone is too slow. Using the 1 cm and 2 cm cube figures makes the point clearly.

notes.h: Advantages and disadvantages of being multicellular
notes.b: Being made of many specialised cells brings benefits, but it also has costs. Comparing the two shows why both unicellular and multicellular life exist.
points: Advantage: a larger size, which means fewer predators and access to light or food.
Advantage: cells inside the body are protected from the environment, because they are surrounded by other cells.
Advantage: efficiency from specialisation, since each cell type does one job well.
Advantage: the organism can survive the death of individual cells, which are replaced.
Disadvantage: more energy and resources are needed to build and maintain the body.
Disadvantage: damage to one vital organ or system can kill the whole organism, because the other cells depend on it.
Disadvantage: growth to reproductive age takes longer than for unicellular organisms, which can divide within hours.
notes.tip: Give advantages and disadvantages as paired points with a reason, for example specialisation is efficient, but one failed vital organ can be fatal.

keyTerms.definition: A group of similar cells with the same structure working together to carry out a particular function.
A structure made of several different tissues working together to carry out one or more functions.
A group of organs working together to carry out a major function.
The process by which cells become specialised, each type using only some of its genes.
An unspecialised cell that can still develop into several cell types.
The surface area of an organism divided by its volume, which falls as the organism gets bigger.
Plant vascular tissue that carries water and minerals.
Plant vascular tissue that carries food.
Dividing plant cells at root and shoot tips where growth happens.
Each cell type doing one job very efficiently while depending on the other cell types.

questions.prompt: Define the terms tissue and organ, and give one example of each from a flowering plant.
questions.model: A tissue is a group of similar cells with the same structure working together to carry out a particular function. For example, xylem vascular tissue carries water and minerals through the plant. An organ is a structure made of several different tissues working together to carry out one or more functions. For example, a leaf is an organ made of dermal, ground and vascular tissue, and it carries out photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Explain why a large multicellular organism needs a transport system but a unicellular organism does not.
questions.model: A unicellular organism has a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion across its membrane is enough to supply oxygen and food and to remove wastes. As an organism gets bigger its volume increases faster than its surface area, so the ratio falls. For example, a 1 cm cube has a ratio of 6:1, while a 2 cm cube has a surface area of 24 cm² and a volume of 8 cm³, a ratio of 3:1. In a large multicellular organism most cells are far from the surface, so diffusion alone is too slow. It therefore needs a transport system, such as blood and the heart in animals or xylem and phloem in plants, to carry materials to and from all its cells.

questions.prompt: Describe the complexity of multicellular organisms, referring to cell specialisation and the levels of organisation.
questions.model: Multicellular organisms are organised in levels of increasing complexity: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and organ systems together make up the organism. For example, a muscle cell forms muscle tissue, which with other tissues forms the stomach, which is part of the digestive system that breaks down and absorbs food in the human body. Each cell is specialised, and differentiation means that cells use only some of their genes so that their structure suits their job. A red blood cell has no nucleus and a biconcave disc shape, giving room for haemoglobin and a large surface area for carrying oxygen; a root hair cell has a long extension giving a large surface area for absorbing water and minerals. Division of labour means each cell type does one job very efficiently, but no cell can survive alone. An advantage of being multicellular is that the organism can survive the death of individual cells, which are replaced. A disadvantage is that damage to one vital organ or system can kill the whole organism.
